question.full_text:
The two nearest harmonics of a tube closed at one end and open at other end are $220\,\mathrm{Hz}$ and $260\,\mathrm{Hz}$. What is the fundamental frequency of the system?
(1) $30\,\mathrm{Hz}$
(2) $40\,\mathrm{Hz}$
(3) $10\,\mathrm{Hz}$
(4) $20\,\mathrm{Hz}$
question.html:
The two nearest harmonics of a tube closed at one end and open at other end are 220 Hz and 260 Hz. What is the fundamental frequency of the system?
  1. (1)30 Hz
  2. (2)40 Hz
  3. (3)10 Hz
  4. (4)20 Hz
question.stem: The two nearest harmonics of a tube closed at one end and open at other end are $220\,\mathrm{Hz}$ and $260\,\mathrm{Hz}$. What is the fundamental frequency of the system?

solution.full_text:
1. Two successive frequencies of closed pipe
2. $\frac{nv}{4l} = 220$ ...(i)
3. $\frac{(n + 2)v}{4l} = 260$ ...(ii)
4. Dividing (ii) by (i), we get
5. $\frac{n + 2}{n} = \frac{260}{220} = \frac{13}{11}$
6. $11n + 22 = 13n$
7. $n = 11$
8. So, $11\frac{v}{4l} = 220$
9. $\frac{v}{4l} = 20$
10. So fundamental frequency is $20\,\mathrm{Hz}$.

  2. nv4l = 220 ...(i)
  3. (n + 2)v4l = 260 ...(ii)
  4. Dividing (ii) by (i), we get
  5. n + 2n = 260220 = 1311
  6. 11n + 22 = 13n
  7. n = 11
  8. So, 11v4l = 220
  9. v4l = 20
  10. So fundamental frequency is 20 Hz.

steps: A tube closed at one end supports only odd harmonics: $f = (2n-1) f_0$.
Two nearest harmonics differ by $2f_0$: $2f_0 = 260\,\mathrm{Hz} - 220\,\mathrm{Hz} = 40\,\mathrm{Hz}$.
Check: $\frac{220}{20} = 11$ and $\frac{260}{20} = 13$ are consecutive odd integers, so $f_0 = 20\,\mathrm{Hz}$, which is option $4$.

solution.full_text:
1. $h_{\mathrm{oil}}\,\rho_{\mathrm{oil}}\,g = h_{\mathrm{water}}\,\rho_{\mathrm{water}}\,g$
2. $140 \times \rho_{\mathrm{oil}} = 130 \times \rho_{\mathrm{water}}$
3. $\rho_{\mathrm{oil}} = \frac{13}{14} \times 1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^{3}}$
4. $\rho_{\mathrm{oil}} = 928\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$
solution.html:
1. hoil ρoil g = hwater ρwater g
  2. 140 × ρoil = 130 × ρwater
  3. ρoil = 1314 × 1000 kg/m3
  4. ρoil = 928 kg m-3
steps: $h_{\mathrm{oil}}\,\rho_{\mathrm{oil}}\,g = h_{\mathrm{water}}\,\rho_{\mathrm{water}}\,g$
$140 \times \rho_{\mathrm{oil}} = 130 \times \rho_{\mathrm{water}}$
$\rho_{\mathrm{oil}} = \frac{13}{14} \times 1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^{3}}$
$\rho_{\mathrm{oil}} = 928\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$
Water rises $65\,\mathrm{mm}$ on the right, so it falls $65\,\mathrm{mm}$ on the oil side; the oil-water interface $B$ is $130\,\mathrm{mm}$ below the final water level $E$.
Oil top $A$ is $10\,\mathrm{mm}$ above $E$, so $h_{oil} = 65 + 65 + 10 = 140\,\mathrm{mm}$.
Water column above level $BC$ on the right: $h_w = 65 + 65 = 130\,\mathrm{mm}$.
Equal pressures at $B$ and $C$: $P_a + \rho_{oil} g h_{oil} = P_a + \rho_w g h_w$.
$\rho_{oil} = \rho_w \frac{h_w}{h_{oil}} = 1000 \times \frac{130}{140} \approx 928.6\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$.
$\approx 928\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, which is option $2$.

  2. Oil top A is 10 mm above E, so hoil = 65 + 65 + 10 = 140 mm.
  3. Water column above level BC on the right: hw = 65 + 65 = 130 mm.
  4. Equal pressures at B and C: Pa + ρoil g hoil = Pa + ρw g hw.
  5. ρoil = ρw hwhoil = 1000 × 130140 ≈ 928.6 kg m-3.
  6. ≈ 928 kg m-3, which is option 2.

question.full_text:
A particle executes linear simple harmonic motion with an amplitude of $3\,\mathrm{cm}$. When the particle is at $2\,\mathrm{cm}$ from the mean position, the magnitude of its velocity is equal to that of its acceleration. Then its time period in seconds is
(1) $\dfrac{4\pi}{\sqrt{5}}$
(2) $\dfrac{2\pi}{\sqrt{3}}$
(3) $\dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{\pi}$
(4) $\dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{2\pi}$
question.html:
A particle executes linear simple harmonic motion with an amplitude of 3 cm. When the particle is at 2 cm from the mean position, the magnitude of its velocity is equal to that of its acceleration. Then its time period in seconds is
  1. (1)4π5
  2. (2)2π3
  3. (3)5π
  4. (4)52π
question.stem: A particle executes linear simple harmonic motion with an amplitude of $3\,\mathrm{cm}$. When the particle is at $2\,\mathrm{cm}$ from the mean position, the magnitude of its velocity is equal to that of its acceleration. Then its time period in seconds is

solution.html:
1. v = ωA2 - x2
  2. a = xω2
  3. v = a
  4. ωA2 - x2 = xω2
  5. (3)2 - (2)2 = 2(2πT)
  6. 5 = 4πT
  7. T = 4π5
steps: $v = \omega\sqrt{A^{2} - x^{2}}$
$a = x\omega^{2}$
$v = a$
$\omega\sqrt{A^{2} - x^{2}} = x\omega^{2}$
$\sqrt{5} = \frac{4\pi}{T}$
$T = \frac{4\pi}{\sqrt{5}}$
In SHM the speed at displacement $x$ is $|v| = \omega\sqrt{A^2 - x^2}$.
With $A = 3\,\mathrm{cm}$ and $x = 2\,\mathrm{cm}$: $|v| = \omega\sqrt{9 - 4} = \sqrt{5}\,\omega$.
The acceleration magnitude is $|a| = \omega^2 x = 2\omega^2$.
Setting $|v| = |a|$: $\sqrt{5}\,\omega = 2\omega^2 \Rightarrow \omega = \frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}\,\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$.
$T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega} = \frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{5}/2} = \frac{4\pi}{\sqrt{5}}\,\mathrm{s}$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. In SHM the speed at displacement x is |v| = ωA2 - x2.
  2. With A = 3 cm and x = 2 cm: |v| = ω9 - 4 = 5 ω.
  3. The acceleration magnitude is |a| = ω2 x = 2ω2.
  4. Setting |v| = |a|: 5 ω = 2ω2 ⇒ ω = 52 rad s-1.
  5. T = 2πω = 2π5/2 = 4π5 s, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: In SHM |v| = omega*sqrt(A^2 - x^2) = omega*sqrt(5) and |a| = omega^2*x = 2*omega^2; equating gives omega = sqrt(5)/2, so T = 2*pi/omega = 4*pi/sqrt(5) s.

question.full_text:
Two astronauts are floating in gravitational free space after having lost contact with their spaceship. The two will:
(1) Move away from each other
(2) Will become stationary
(3) Keep floating at the same distance between them
(4) Move towards each other
question.html:
Two astronauts are floating in gravitational free space after having lost contact with their spaceship. The two will:
  1. (1)Move away from each other
  2. (2)Will become stationary
  3. (3)Keep floating at the same distance between them
  4. (4)Move towards each other
question.stem: Two astronauts are floating in gravitational free space after having lost contact with their spaceship. The two will:

options.text: Keep floating at the same distance between them

solution.full_text:
1. Both the astronauts are in the condition of weightness.
2. Gravitational force between them pulls towards each other.
solution.html:
1. Both the astronauts are in the condition of weightness.
  2. Gravitational force between them pulls towards each other.
steps: Both the astronauts are in the condition of weightness.
Gravitational force between them pulls towards each other.
printed_lines: Both the astronauts are in the condition of
weightness. Gravitational force between them pulls

steps: In gravitational free space there is no external gravitational field, so $\vec{F}_{\text{ext}} = 0$.
The two astronauts still attract each other with $F = \frac{G m_1 m_2}{r^2}$, directed along the line joining them.
This attraction is unopposed, so each accelerates towards the other while the centre of mass stays fixed; they move towards each other, which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:

  2. The two astronauts still attract each other with F = G m1 m2r2, directed along the line joining them.
  3. This attraction is unopposed, so each accelerates towards the other while the centre of mass stays fixed; they move towards each other, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: With no external gravity, the only force on each astronaut is their mutual gravitational attraction, so starting from rest they slowly move towards each other.

question.full_text:
The de-Broglie wavelength of a neutron in thermal equilibrium with heavy water at a temperature $T$ (Kelvin) and mass $m$, is
(1) $\dfrac{2h}{\sqrt{3mkT}}$
(2) $\dfrac{2h}{\sqrt{mkT}}$
(3) $\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{mkT}}$
(4) $\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3mkT}}$
question.html:
The de-Broglie wavelength of a neutron in thermal equilibrium with heavy water at a temperature T (Kelvin) and mass m, is
  1. (1)2h3mkT
  2. (2)2hmkT
  3. (3)hmkT
  4. (4)h3mkT
question.stem: The de-Broglie wavelength of a neutron in thermal equilibrium with heavy water at a temperature $T$ (Kelvin) and mass $m$, is

solution.full_text:
1. de-Broglie wavelength
2. $\lambda = \frac{h}{mv}$
3. $= \frac{h}{\sqrt{2m(\mathrm{KE})}}$
4. $= \frac{h}{\sqrt{2m(\frac{3}{2}kT)}}$
5. $\lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{3mkT}}$
solution.html:
1. de-Broglie wavelength
  2. λ = hmv
  3. = h2m(KE)
  4. = h2m(32kT)
  5. λ = h3mkT
steps: de-Broglie wavelength
$\lambda = \frac{h}{mv}$
$= \frac{h}{\sqrt{2m(\mathrm{KE})}}$
$= \frac{h}{\sqrt{2m(\frac{3}{2}kT)}}$
$\lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{3mkT}}$
In thermal equilibrium at temperature $T$, the mean kinetic energy of the neutron is $E = \frac{3}{2}kT$.
Momentum from kinetic energy: $p = \sqrt{2mE}$.
$p = \sqrt{2m \cdot \frac{3}{2}kT} = \sqrt{3mkT}$.
$\lambda = \frac{h}{p} = \frac{h}{\sqrt{3mkT}}$, which is option $4$.

steps: Initial energy of the isolated charged capacitor: $U = \frac{Q^2}{2C}$.
With the battery removed, the total charge $Q$ is conserved when the identical uncharged capacitor is connected.
Two identical capacitors in parallel give $C' = C + C = 2C$.
Final energy: $U' = \frac{Q^2}{2C'} = \frac{Q^2}{2(2C)} = \frac{Q^2}{4C}$.
$\frac{U'}{U} = \frac{Q^2/4C}{Q^2/2C} = \frac{1}{2}$, so the energy decreases by a factor of $2$, which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Initial energy of the isolated charged capacitor: U = Q22C.
  2. With the battery removed, the total charge Q is conserved when the identical uncharged capacitor is connected.
  3. Two identical capacitors in parallel give C' = C + C = 2C.
  4. Final energy: U' = Q22C' = Q22(2C) = Q24C.
  5. U'U = Q2/4CQ2/2C = 12, so the energy decreases by a factor of 2, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: Charge Q is conserved and shared over capacitance 2C, so U' = Q^2/(2*2C) = U/2: energy decreases by a factor of 2.

subtopics.name: Redistribution of Charges
subtopics.why: The answer depends on charge sharing between a charged and an identical uncharged capacitor (charge conserved, common potential halves), which makes the total energy Q^2/2(2C), half the original.

step_list: Recognise that with the battery removed the charge Q on the system is conserved (not the voltage)
Find the equivalent capacitance of the two identical capacitors in parallel (C becomes 2C)
Apply U = Q^2/2C with the conserved charge and new capacitance and compare with the initial energy
difficulty.why: The work is identifying the conserved quantity (charge) after isolation, combining the capacitances in parallel, and substituting into the energy formula written in terms of Q to get the ratio.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: Trap option: using U = CV^2/2 while wrongly holding V fixed (as if the battery were still connected) gives exactly one of the listed options, so the choice of which quantity is conserved decides the answer.

categories.concept: Once the battery is gone the charge is fixed, so sharing it with an equal capacitor doubles C at constant Q and halves $U=\frac{Q^2}{2C}$

trap.label: condition_missed
trap.route: The voltage is held at its old value, as though the battery were still across the plates, and $U=\frac12CV^2$ with C doubled then reads as twice the energy; the stem's 'The battery is removed' is exactly what forbids holding V fixed.
trap.who: a student who reaches for $U=\frac12CV^2$ and keeps V at the battery's emf out of habit
trap.feels: the capacitance plainly doubles, and with V fixed the energy formula is linear in C, so a factor of 2 looks forced on you

steps.text: Two identical capacitors in parallel give a total capacitance of 2C.
V is unchanged, so $U=\frac12(2C)V^2$ is twice the original energy.
steps.fix: With the battery removed it is Q that is fixed, not V; the charge spreads over twice the capacitance so the shared voltage falls to $V/2$.

other_options.who: a student who has just used conservation of charge to do the redistribution and carries the same bookkeeping over to the energy
other_options.feels: nothing leaves the pair of capacitors and the charge is conserved, so the stored energy looks like it must be conserved with it

steps.text: The charge Q is conserved when the uncharged capacitor is connected.
Nothing escaped, so the stored energy stays the same.
steps.fix: Charge is conserved here and energy is not: half of it is lost in the connecting wires as the charge flows, which is why $\frac{Q^2}{2(2C)}$ is half of $\frac{Q^2}{2C}$.

other_options.proof: $U=\frac{Q^2}{2C}$ quadruples only if Q doubles while C is held fixed. The stem fixes the opposite: the added capacitor is 'identical', so C doubles, and 'uncharged', so Q does not change. Neither $\frac{Q^2}{2C}$ nor $\frac12CV^2$ returns a factor of 4 under the stem's own substitution; the option sits beside option 2 as the other 'increases' entry.

1. $\lambda_0 = 3250 \times 10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m}$
2. $\lambda = 2536 \times 10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m}$
3. $\phi = \frac{1242\,\mathrm{eV\text{-}nm}}{325\,\mathrm{nm}} = 3.82\,\mathrm{eV}$
4. $h\nu = \frac{1242\,\mathrm{eV\text{-}nm}}{253.6\,\mathrm{nm}} = 4.89\,\mathrm{eV}$
5. $\mathrm{KE_{max}} = (4.89 - 3.82)\,\mathrm{eV} = 1.077\,\mathrm{eV}$
6. $\frac{1}{2}mv^{2} = 1.077 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}$
7. $v = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 1.077 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}}{9.1 \times 10^{-31}}}$
8. $v = 0.6 \times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{m/s}$
solution.html:
1. λ0 = 3250 × 10-10 m
  2. λ = 2536 × 10-10 m
  3. φ = 1242 eV-nm325 nm = 3.82 eV
  4. hν = 1242 eV-nm253.6 nm = 4.89 eV
  5. KEmax = (4.89 - 3.82) eV = 1.077 eV
  6. 12mv2 = 1.077 × 1.6 × 10-19
  7. v = 2 × 1.077 × 1.6 × 10-199.1 × 10-31
  8. v = 0.6 × 106 m/s
steps: $\lambda_0 = 3250 \times 10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m}$
$\lambda = 2536 \times 10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m}$
$\phi = \frac{1242\,\mathrm{eV\text{-}nm}}{325\,\mathrm{nm}} = 3.82\,\mathrm{eV}$
$h\nu = \frac{1242\,\mathrm{eV\text{-}nm}}{253.6\,\mathrm{nm}} = 4.89\,\mathrm{eV}$
$\mathrm{KE_{max}} = (4.89 - 3.82)\,\mathrm{eV} = 1.077\,\mathrm{eV}$
$v = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 1.077 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}}{9.1 \times 10^{-31}}}$
$v = 0.6 \times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{m/s}$
$hc = 4.14 \times 10^{-15}\,\mathrm{eV\,s} \times 3 \times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} = 1.242 \times 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{eV\,m}$.
Photon energy: $E = \frac{hc}{\lambda} = \frac{1.242 \times 10^{-6}}{2536 \times 10^{-10}} \approx 4.898\,\mathrm{eV}$.
Work function: $\phi_0 = \frac{hc}{\lambda_0} = \frac{1.242 \times 10^{-6}}{3250 \times 10^{-10}} \approx 3.822\,\mathrm{eV}$.
Einstein's equation: $K_{max} = E - \phi_0 = 4.898 - 3.822 \approx 1.076\,\mathrm{eV}$.
Convert to joules: $K_{max} = 1.076 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \approx 1.722 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$.
$v = \sqrt{\frac{2K_{max}}{m_e}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 1.722 \times 10^{-19}}{9.1 \times 10^{-31}}} = \sqrt{3.784 \times 10^{11}} \approx 6.15 \times 10^{5}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
$6.15 \times 10^{5} \approx 0.6 \times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} = 6 \times 10^{5}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, which matches both option $3$ and option $4$; option $4$ chosen.
ai_solution.html:
1. hc = 4.14 × 10-15 eV s × 3 × 108 m s-1 = 1.242 × 10-6 eV m.
  2. Photon energy: E = hcλ = 1.242 × 10-62536 × 10-10 ≈ 4.898 eV.
  3. Work function: φ0 = hcλ0 = 1.242 × 10-63250 × 10-10 ≈ 3.822 eV.
  4. Einstein's equation: Kmax = E - φ0 = 4.898 - 3.822 ≈ 1.076 eV.
  5. Convert to joules: Kmax = 1.076 × 1.6 × 10-19 ≈ 1.722 × 10-19 J.
  6. v = 2Kmaxme = 2 × 1.722 × 10-199.1 × 10-31 = 3.784 × 1011 ≈ 6.15 × 105 m s-1.
  7. 6.15 × 105 ≈ 0.6 × 106 m s-1 = 6 × 105 m s-1, which matches both option 3 and option 4; option 4 chosen.
ai_solution.why: KE = hc/lambda - hc/lambda0 = 4.898 - 3.822 = 1.076 eV, so v = sqrt(2KE/m) = 6.15 x 10^5 m/s; options 3 and 4 are numerically the same value.

step_list: Recognise that the source (first car, 22 m/s) and the observer (second car, 16.5 m/s) are both moving towards each other, and pick the matching signs in the Doppler formula: observer speed added in the numerator, source speed subtracted in the denominator
Substitute v = 340, v_o = 16.5, v_s = 22 and f = 400 Hz into f' = f (v + v_o)/(v - v_s)
Evaluate the ratio 356.5/318 times 400 and match it to the nearest option

difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: The Doppler effect section has been dropped from the current rationalised NCERT Class 11 Physics, so a candidate preparing only from the current NCERT may not have the formula or its sign convention.

trap.feels: 361 Hz is a shifted frequency, not the horn's own 400 Hz, so it reads as the result of having done the Doppler work

steps.text: Both motions must be put in: the listener's speed in the numerator, the source's in the denominator.
Write $f'=f\frac{v-v_o}{v+v_s}=400\times\frac{323.5}{362}=357$ Hz and take the nearest printed option, 361 Hz.
steps.fix: The cars approach, so the gap closes: the listener's speed is added and the source's subtracted, giving $400\times\frac{340+16.5}{340-22}=448$ Hz. A pitch below 400 Hz can only mean separation.

other_options.who: a student who takes both speeds subtractively, as in the single-moving-source form, and so corrects the numerator the wrong way
other_options.feels: 411 Hz is above the horn's frequency, which matches the approach, and it is less than 448 Hz so it looks like the more careful of the two raised values

steps.text: Write $f'=f\frac{v-v_o}{v-v_s}=400\times\frac{323.5}{318}=407$ Hz and read it as the 411 Hz option.
steps.fix: A listener moving towards the source meets more wavefronts per second, so that speed is added: the numerator is $340+16.5$, not $340-16.5$.

other_options.proof: Ran the stem's four numbers (400 Hz, 340, 22, 16.5 m/s) through the Doppler relation in every sign combination: 448 (the key), 427.7 (source only), 419.4 (listener only), 406.9, 393.9 and 357.5 Hz. The closest any of them comes to 350 Hz is the 357.5 Hz inverted-sign value, which is 7.5 Hz away and 3.5 Hz from option 4; nothing lands on 350. It widens the spread below 400 Hz.

categories.note: None of the three wrong options is the exact output of a Doppler substitution; each route above is quoted with the value it actually computes (357 Hz for option 4, 407 Hz for option 1) so a reviewer can audit the few-hertz gap to the printed figure. categories.concept: Turning a mirror through an angle turns the reflected beam through twice that angle, so the spot's shift is $y=x\tan2\theta\approx2x\theta$

steps.text: The spot moves y on a scale a distance x from the mirror, so the beam has swung through an angle whose tangent is $y/x$.
The mirror turned through that same angle, so $\theta=\frac{y}{x}$.
steps.fix: Rotating a mirror by $\theta$ rotates the reflected beam by $2\theta$, because both the normal and the angle of reflection move; so $2\theta=y/x$ and $\theta=\frac{y}{2x}$.

other_options.who: a student who keeps the factor 2 but builds the tangent with the distance to the mirror over the displacement of the spot
other_options.feels: x is the big printed distance and y the small shift, so writing the ratio as $x/y$ looks like the natural way round, and the 2 being there suggests the reflection law was used

So $\tan2\theta=\frac{x}{y}$ and $\theta=\frac{x}{2y}$.
steps.fix: y is the side opposite the angle and x the adjacent one, so $\tan2\theta=y/x$; as a check, $\theta$ must shrink when y shrinks, and $x/2y$ grows.

question.full_text:
Young’s double slit experiment is first performed in air and then in a medium other than air. It is found that $8^{\mathrm{th}}$ bright fringe in the medium lies where $5^{\mathrm{th}}$ dark fringe lies in air. The refractive index of the medium is nearly
(1) $1.69$
(2) $1.78$
(3) $1.25$
(4) $1.59$

question.stem: Young’s double slit experiment is first performed in air and then in a medium other than air. It is found that $8^{\mathrm{th}}$ bright fringe in the medium lies where $5^{\mathrm{th}}$ dark fringe lies in air. The refractive index of the medium is nearly

solution.full_text:
1. $X_1 = X_{5\text{th dark}} = (2 \times 5 - 1)\frac{\lambda D}{2d}$
2. $X_2 = X_{8\text{th bright}} = 8\frac{\lambda D}{\mu d}$
3. $X_1 = X_2$
4. $\frac{9}{2}\frac{\cancel{\lambda D}}{\cancel{d}} = 8\frac{\cancel{\lambda D}}{\mu \cancel{d}}$
5. $\mu = \frac{16}{9} = 1.78$
solution.html:
1. X1 = X5th dark = (2 × 5 - 1)λ D2d
  2. X2 = X8th bright = 8λ Dμ d
  3. X1 = X2
  4. 92λ Dd = 8λ Dμ d
  5. μ = 169 = 1.78
steps: $X_1 = X_{5\text{th dark}} = (2 \times 5 - 1)\frac{\lambda D}{2d}$
$X_2 = X_{8\text{th bright}} = 8\frac{\lambda D}{\mu d}$
$\frac{9}{2}\frac{\cancel{\lambda D}}{\cancel{d}} = 8\frac{\cancel{\lambda D}}{\mu \cancel{d}}$
In the medium the wavelength becomes $\lambda' = \frac{\lambda}{\mu}$.
Position of the $8^{\mathrm{th}}$ bright fringe in the medium: $y_8 = \frac{8\lambda' D}{d} = \frac{8\lambda D}{\mu d}$.
Position of the $5^{\mathrm{th}}$ dark fringe in air: $y_5 = \frac{(2 \times 5 - 1)\lambda D}{2d} = \frac{4.5\,\lambda D}{d}$.
Equate the two positions: $\frac{8\lambda D}{\mu d} = \frac{4.5\,\lambda D}{d}$.
$\mu = \frac{8}{4.5} = \frac{16}{9} \approx 1.78$, which is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. In the medium the wavelength becomes λ' = λμ.
  2. Position of the 8th bright fringe in the medium: y8 = 8λ' Dd = 8λ Dμ d.
  3. Position of the 5th dark fringe in air: y5 = (2 × 5 - 1)λ D2d = 4.5 λ Dd.
  4. Equate the two positions: 8λ Dμ d = 4.5 λ Dd.
  5. μ = 84.5 = 169 ≈ 1.78, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: 8th bright in medium at 8(lambda/mu)D/d equals 5th dark in air at 4.5 lambda D/d, so mu = 8/4.5 = 1.78.

question.stem: A spring of force constant $k$ is cut into lengths of ratio $1 : 2 : 3$. They are connected in series and the new force constant is $k'$. Then they are connected in parallel and force constant is $k''$. Then $k' : k''$ is

solution.full_text:
1. Spring constant $\propto \frac{1}{\text{length}}$
2. $k \propto \frac{1}{l}$
3. i.e, $k_1 = 6k$
4. $k_2 = 3k$
5. $k_3 = 2k$
6. In series
7. $\frac{1}{k'} = \frac{1}{6k} + \frac{1}{3k} + \frac{1}{2k}$
8. $\frac{1}{k'} = \frac{6}{6k}$
9. $k' = k$
10. $k'' = 6k + 3k + 2k$
11. $k'' = 11k$
12. $\frac{k'}{\ } = \frac{1}{11}$ i.e $k' : k'' = 1 : 11$
solution.html:
1. Spring constant ∝ 1length
  2. k ∝ 1l
  3. i.e, k1 = 6k
  4. k2 = 3k
  5. k3 = 2k
  6. In series
  7. 1k' = 16k + 13k + 12k
  8. 1k' = 66k
  9. k' = k
  10. k'' = 6k + 3k + 2k
  11. k'' = 11k
  12. k'  = 111 i.e k' : k'' = 1 : 11
steps: Spring constant $\propto \frac{1}{\text{length}}$
$k \propto \frac{1}{l}$
In series
For a uniform spring $k \propto \frac{1}{l}$, i.e. $kl = \text{constant}$.
Lengths in ratio $1:2:3$ give $l_1 = \frac{l}{6},\ l_2 = \frac{l}{3},\ l_3 = \frac{l}{2}$.
Series: $\frac{1}{k'} = \frac{1}{6k} + \frac{1}{3k} + \frac{1}{2k} = \frac{1+2+3}{6k} = \frac{1}{k}$, so $k' = k$.
Parallel: $k'' = 6k + 3k + 2k = 11k$.
$k' : k'' = k : 11k = 1 : 11$, which is option $1$.

  2. Lengths in ratio 1:2:3 give l1 = l6, l2 = l3, l3 = l2.
  3. So k1 = 6k, k2 = 3k, k3 = 2k.
  4. Series: 1k' = 16k + 13k + 12k = 1+2+36k = 1k, so k' = k.
  5. Parallel: k'' = 6k + 3k + 2k = 11k.
  6. k' : k'' = k : 11k = 1 : 11, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: Spring constant varies inversely with length, so the pieces are 6k, 3k and 2k; in series they give back k, in parallel 11k, so k':k'' = 1:11.

A thin prism having refracting angle $10^\circ$ is made of glass of refractive index $1.42$. This prism is combined with another thin prism of glass of refractive index $1.7$. This combination produces dispersion without deviation. The refracting angle of second prism should be
(1) $8^\circ$
(2) $10^\circ$
(3) $4^\circ$
(4) $6^\circ$

question.stem: A thin prism having refracting angle $10^\circ$ is made of glass of refractive index $1.42$. This prism is combined with another thin prism of glass of refractive index $1.7$. This combination produces dispersion without deviation. The refracting angle of second prism should be

solution.html:
1. (μ - 1)A + (μ' - 1)A' = 0
  2. |(μ - 1)A| = |(μ' - 1)A'|
  3. (1.42 - 1)× 10° = (1.7 - 1)A'
  4. 4.2 = 0.7A'
  5. A' = 6°
steps: $A' = 6^\circ$
For a thin prism the deviation is $\delta = (\mu - 1)A$.
The prisms are placed in opposite orientation, so zero net deviation requires $\delta_1 = \delta_2$, i.e. $(\mu_1 - 1)A_1 = (\mu_2 - 1)A_2$.
$\delta_1 = (1.42 - 1)\times 10^\circ = 4.2^\circ$.
$(1.7 - 1)A_2 = 4.2^\circ \Rightarrow A_2 = \frac{4.2^\circ}{0.7} = 6^\circ$, which is option $4$.

  3. δ1 = (1.42 - 1)× 10° = 4.2°.
  4. (1.7 - 1)A2 = 4.2° ⇒ A2 = 4.2°0.7 = 6°, which is option 4.

question.full_text:
A gas mixture consists of 2 moles of $\mathrm{O_2}$ and 4 moles of Ar at temperature $T$. Neglecting all vibrational modes, the total internal energy of the system is
(1) $9\,RT$
(2) $11\,RT$
(3) $4\,RT$
(4) $15\,RT$
question.html:
A gas mixture consists of 2 moles of O2 and 4 moles of Ar at temperature T. Neglecting all vibrational modes, the total internal energy of the system is
  1. (1)9 RT
  2. (2)11 RT
  3. (3)4 RT
  4. (4)15 RT
question.stem: A gas mixture consists of 2 moles of $\mathrm{O_2}$ and 4 moles of Ar at temperature $T$. Neglecting all vibrational modes, the total internal energy of the system is

solution.html:
1. U = n1f12RT + n2f22RT
  2. = 2 × 52RT + 4 × 32RT
  3. = 5 RT + 6 RT
  4. U = 11 RT
steps: $U = n_1\frac{f_1}{2}RT + n_2\frac{f_2}{2}RT$
$= 2 \times \frac{5}{2}RT + 4 \times \frac{3}{2}RT$
Neglecting vibration, $\mathrm{O_2}$ (diatomic) has $f_1 = 5$ degrees of freedom and Ar (monatomic) has $f_2 = 3$.
Total internal energy $U = n_1\frac{f_1}{2}RT + n_2\frac{f_2}{2}RT$.
$U_{\mathrm{O_2}} = 2 \times \frac{5}{2}RT = 5RT$.
$U_{\mathrm{Ar}} = 4 \times \frac{3}{2}RT = 6RT$.
$U = 5RT + 6RT = 11RT$, which is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:

  2. Total internal energy U = n1f12RT + n2f22RT.
  3. UO2 = 2 × 52RT = 5RT.
  4. UAr = 4 × 32RT = 6RT.
  5. U = 5RT + 6RT = 11RT, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: O2 diatomic has 5 degrees of freedom (no vibration), Ar monatomic has 3: U = 2(5/2)RT + 4(3/2)RT = 5RT + 6RT = 11RT.

(1) $-4\,\mathrm{m/s^{2}}$
(2) $-8\,\mathrm{m/s^{2}}$
(3) $0$
(4) $5\,\mathrm{m/s^{2}}$
question.html:
The x and y coordinates of the particle at any time are x = 5t - 2t2 and y = 10t respectively, where x and y are in meters and t in seconds. The acceleration of the particle at t = 2 s is
  1. (1)-4 m/s2
  2. (2)-8 m/s2
  3. (3)0

question.stem: The $x$ and $y$ coordinates of the particle at any time are $x = 5t - 2t^{2}$ and $y = 10t$ respectively, where $x$ and $y$ are in meters and $t$ in seconds. The acceleration of the particle at $t = 2\,\mathrm{s}$ is

solution.full_text:
1. $x = 5t - 2t^{2}$, $y = 10t$
2. $\frac{dx}{dt} = 5 - 4t$, $\frac{dy}{dt} = 10$
3. $v_{x} = 5 - 4t$, $v_{y} = 10$
4. $\frac{dv}{dt}x = -4$, $\frac{dv}{dt}y = 10$
5. $a_{x} = -4$, $a_{y} = 0$
6. Acceleration of particle at $t = 2\,\mathrm{s}$ is $= -4\,\mathrm{m/s^{2}}$

  2. dxdt = 5 - 4t, dydt = 10
  3. vx = 5 - 4t, vy = 10
  4. dvdtx = -4, dvdty = 10
  5. ax = -4, ay = 0
  6. Acceleration of particle at t = 2 s is = -4 m/s2

$v_y = \frac{dy}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt}(10t) = 10\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
$a_y = \frac{dv_y}{dt} = 0$.
$\vec{a} = a_x\hat{i} + a_y\hat{j} = -4\hat{i}\,\mathrm{m/s^{2}}$, so at $t = 2\,\mathrm{s}$ the acceleration is $-4\,\mathrm{m/s^{2}}$, which is option $1$.

question.full_text:
Two discs of same moment of inertia rotating about their regular axis passing through centre and perpendicular to the plane of disc with angular velocities $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$. They are brought into contact face to face coinciding the axis of rotation. The expression for loss of energy during this process is
(1) $I(\omega_1 - \omega_2)^2$
(2) $\frac{I}{8}(\omega_1 - \omega_2)^2$
(3) $\frac{1}{2}I(\omega_1 + \omega_2)^2$
(4) $\frac{1}{4}I(\omega_1 - \omega_2)^2$
question.html:
Two discs of same moment of inertia rotating about their regular axis passing through centre and perpendicular to the plane of disc with angular velocities ω1 and ω2. They are brought into contact face to face coinciding the axis of rotation. The expression for loss of energy during this process is
  1. (1)I(ω1 - ω2)2
  2. (2)I8(ω1 - ω2)2
  3. (3)12I(ω1 + ω2)2
  4. (4)14I(ω1 - ω2)2
question.stem: Two discs of same moment of inertia rotating about their regular axis passing through centre and perpendicular to the plane of disc with angular velocities $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$. They are brought into contact face to face coinciding the axis of rotation. The expression for loss of energy during this process is

solution.full_text:
1. $\Delta \mathrm{KE} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{I_1 I_2}{I_1 + I_2}(\omega_1 - \omega_2)^2$
2. $= \frac{1}{2}\frac{I^2}{(2I)}(\omega_1 - \omega_2)^2$
3. $= \frac{1}{4}I(\omega_1 - \omega_2)^2$
solution.html:
1. Δ KE = 12I1 I2I1 + I2(ω1 - ω2)2
  2. = 12I2(2I)(ω1 - ω2)2
  3. = 14I(ω1 - ω2)2
steps: $\Delta \mathrm{KE} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{I_1 I_2}{I_1 + I_2}(\omega_1 - \omega_2)^2$
$= \frac{1}{4}I(\omega_1 - \omega_2)^2$
No external torque acts, so angular momentum is conserved: $I\omega_1 + I\omega_2 = 2I\omega$.
$\omega = \frac{\omega_1 + \omega_2}{2}$.
Initial kinetic energy: $K_i = \frac{1}{2}I\omega_1^2 + \frac{1}{2}I\omega_2^2 = \frac{1}{2}I(\omega_1^2 + \omega_2^2)$.
Final kinetic energy: $K_f = \frac{1}{2}(2I)\left(\frac{\omega_1 + \omega_2}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{4}I(\omega_1 + \omega_2)^2$.
$\Delta K = K_i - K_f = \frac{1}{4}I\left[2\omega_1^2 + 2\omega_2^2 - (\omega_1 + \omega_2)^2\right]$.
$\Delta K = \frac{1}{4}I(\omega_1^2 - 2\omega_1\omega_2 + \omega_2^2) = \frac{1}{4}I(\omega_1 - \omega_2)^2$, which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. No external torque acts, so angular momentum is conserved: Iω1 + Iω2 = 2Iω.
  2. ω = ω1 + ω22.
  3. Initial kinetic energy: Ki = 12Iω12 + 12Iω22 = 12I(ω12 + ω22).
  4. Final kinetic energy: Kf = 12(2I)(ω1 + ω22)2 = 14I(ω1 + ω2)2.
  5. Δ K = Ki - Kf = 14I[2ω12 + 2ω22 - (ω1 + ω2)2].
  6. Δ K = 14I(ω12 - 2ω1ω2 + ω22) = 14I(ω1 - ω2)2, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: Angular momentum conserved gives common omega = (w1+w2)/2; KE loss = (1/2)I(w1^2+w2^2) - (1/4)I(w1+w2)^2 = (1/4)I(w1-w2)^2.

steps.text: Angular momentum is conserved, so the pair ends at one common $\omega$ and energy is lost.

$I_{eff}$ is the moment of the joined discs, $2I$, so the loss is $\frac{1}{2}(2I)(\omega_1-\omega_2)^2 = I(\omega_1-\omega_2)^2$.

question.full_text:
The bulk modulus of a spherical object is ‘$B$’. If it is subjected to uniform pressure ‘$p$’, the fractional decrease in radius is
(1) $\dfrac{3p}{B}$
(2) $\dfrac{p}{3B}$
(3) $\dfrac{p}{B}$
(4) $\dfrac{B}{3p}$
question.html:
The bulk modulus of a spherical object is ‘B’. If it is subjected to uniform pressure ‘p’, the fractional decrease in radius is
  1. (1)3pB
  2. (2)p3B
  3. (3)pB
  4. (4)B3p
question.stem: The bulk modulus of a spherical object is ‘$B$’. If it is subjected to uniform pressure ‘$p$’, the fractional decrease in radius is

solution.full_text:
1. $B = \frac{p}{\left(\frac{\Delta V}{V}\right)}$
2. $\frac{\Delta V}{V} = \frac{p}{B}$
3. $3\frac{\Delta r}{r} = \frac{p}{B}$
4. $\frac{\Delta r}{r} = \frac{p}{3B}$
solution.html:
1. B = p(Δ VV)
  2. Δ VV = pB
  3. 3Δ rr = pB
  4. Δ rr = p3B
steps: $B = \frac{p}{\left(\frac{\Delta V}{V}\right)}$
$\frac{\Delta V}{V} = \frac{p}{B}$
$3\frac{\Delta r}{r} = \frac{p}{B}$
$\frac{\Delta r}{r} = \frac{p}{3B}$
By definition of bulk modulus, $B = \frac{p}{\Delta V / V}$, so $\frac{\Delta V}{V} = \frac{p}{B}$.
For a sphere $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$, so $\frac{\Delta V}{V} = 3\frac{\Delta r}{r}$.
Equating, $3\frac{\Delta r}{r} = \frac{p}{B}$.
$\frac{\Delta r}{r} = \frac{p}{3B}$, which is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. By definition of bulk modulus, B = pΔ V / V, so Δ VV = pB.
  2. For a sphere V = 43π r3, so Δ VV = 3Δ rr.
  3. Equating, 3Δ rr = pB.
  4. Δ rr = p3B, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: B = p/(dV/V) and dV/V = 3 dr/r for a sphere, so dr/r = p/(3B).

solution.full_text:
1. Velocity of girl w.r.t. elevator $= \frac{d}{t_1} = v_{ge}$
2. Velocity of elevator w.r.t. ground $v_{eG} = \frac{d}{t_2}$
3. then velocity of girl w.r.t. ground $\vec{v}_{gG} = \vec{v}_{ge} + \vec{v}_{eG}$
4. i.e, $v_{gG} = v_{ge} + v_{eG}$
5. $\frac{d}{t} = \frac{d}{t_1} + \frac{d}{t_2}$
6. $\frac{1}{t} = \frac{1}{t_1} + \frac{1}{t_2}$
7. $t = \frac{t_1 t_2}{(t_1 + t_2)}$

1. Velocity of girl w.r.t. elevator = dt1 = vge
  2. Velocity of elevator w.r.t. ground veG = dt2
  3. then velocity of girl w.r.t. ground →vgG = →vge + →veG
  4. i.e, vgG = vge + veG
  5. dt = dt1 + dt2
  6. 1t = 1t1 + 1t2
  7. t = t1 t2(t1 + t2)
steps: Velocity of girl w.r.t. elevator $= \frac{d}{t_1} = v_{ge}$
Velocity of elevator w.r.t. ground $v_{eG} = \frac{d}{t_2}$
then velocity of girl w.r.t. ground $\vec{v}_{gG} = \vec{v}_{ge} + \vec{v}_{eG}$
i.e, $v_{gG} = v_{ge} + v_{eG}$
$\frac{d}{t} = \frac{d}{t_1} + \frac{d}{t_2}$
Let the escalator length be $L$. Her walking speed relative to the escalator is $v_1 = \frac{L}{t_1}$.
The escalator's speed is $v_2 = \frac{L}{t_2}$.
Walking up the moving escalator, the speeds add: $v = v_1 + v_2 = \frac{L}{t_1} + \frac{L}{t_2} = \frac{L(t_1 + t_2)}{t_1 t_2}$.
$t = \frac{L}{v} = \frac{t_1 t_2}{t_1 + t_2}$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:

  2. The escalator's speed is v2 = Lt2.
  3. Walking up the moving escalator, the speeds add: v = v1 + v2 = Lt1 + Lt2 = L(t1 + t2)t1 t2.
  4. t = Lv = t1 t2t1 + t2, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: Her speed L/t1 and the escalator's speed L/t2 add, so t = L/(L/t1 + L/t2) = t1 t2/(t1 + t2).

(2) $1800$
(3) $225$
(4) $450$
question.html:
A spherical black body with a radius of 12 cm radiates 450 watt power at 500 K. If the radius were halved and the temperature doubled, the power radiated in watt would be
  1. (1)1000
  2. (2)1800

question.stem: A spherical black body with a radius of $12\,\mathrm{cm}$ radiates $450\,\mathrm{watt}$ power at $500\,\mathrm{K}$. If the radius were halved and the temperature doubled, the power radiated in watt would be

solution.html:
1. Rate of power loss
  2. r ∝ R2T4
  3. r1r2 = R12T14R22T24
  4. = 4 × 116
  5. 450r2 = 14
  6. r2 = 1800 watt
steps: Rate of power loss
$r \propto R^{2}T^{4}$
$= 4 \times \frac{1}{16}$
$r_2 = 1800\,\mathrm{watt}$
By the Stefan-Boltzmann law for a black sphere, $P = \sigma (4\pi r^2) T^4$, so $P \propto r^2 T^4$.
$\frac{P'}{P} = \left(\frac{r'}{r}\right)^2 \left(\frac{T'}{T}\right)^4 = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 (2)^4$.
$P' = 4 \times 450\,\mathrm{W} = 1800\,\mathrm{W}$, which is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. By the Stefan-Boltzmann law for a black sphere, P = σ (4π r2) T4, so P ∝ r2 T4.
  2. P'P = (r'r)2 (T'T)4 = (12)2 (2)4.
  3. (12)2 (2)4 = 14 × 16 = 4.
  4. P' = 4 × 450 W = 1800 W, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: Stefan-Boltzmann: P is proportional to r^2 T^4, so P' = 450 x (1/2)^2 x 2^4 = 450 x 4 = 1800 W.

solution.full_text: 1. Centripetal force $\left(\frac{mv^{2}}{l}\right)$ is provided by tension so the net force will be equal to tension i.e., $T$.

steps: Vertically, the normal reaction balances gravity: $N - mg = 0$.
The table is smooth, so there is no friction; the only horizontal force is the tension $T$, directed toward the peg (centre).
Net force toward the centre: $F_{net} = T$, which provides the centripetal force, $T = \frac{mv^{2}}{l}$.
So the net force is $T$, which is option $3$.

question.stem: In a common emitter transistor amplifier the audio signal voltage across the collector is $3\,\mathrm{V}$. The resistance of collector is $3\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$. If current gain is $100$ and the base resistance is $2\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$, the voltage and power gain of the amplifier is

solution.full_text:
1. Current gain $(\beta) = 100$
2. Voltage gain $(A_V) = \beta\frac{R_c}{R_b}$
3. $= 100\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)$
4. $= 150$
5. Power gain $= A_V\,\beta$
6. $= 150\,(100)$
7. $= 15000$
solution.html:
1. Current gain (β) = 100
  2. Voltage gain (AV) = βRcRb
  3. = 100(32)
  4. = 150
  5. Power gain = AV β
  6. = 150 (100)
  7. = 15000
steps: Current gain $(\beta) = 100$
Voltage gain $(A_V) = \beta\frac{R_c}{R_b}$
$= 100\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)$
Power gain $= A_V\,\beta$
For a common emitter amplifier, voltage gain $A_v = \beta \frac{R_C}{R_B}$.
$A_v = 100 \times \frac{3\,\mathrm{k\Omega}}{2\,\mathrm{k\Omega}} = 150$.
Power gain $A_p = \beta \times A_v$.
$150$ and $15000$ matches option $1$.

  2. Av = 100 × 3 kΩ2 kΩ = 150.

  4. Ap = 100 × 150 = 15000.
  5. 150 and 15000 matches option 1.
ai_solution.why: Voltage gain = beta x Rc/Rb = 100 x 3/2 = 150; power gain = beta x voltage gain = 100 x 150 = 15000.

(2) (c) and (d)
(3) (b) and (d)
(4) (a) and (b)

Which of the following statements are correct?

  2. ((b)) Centre of mass of a body is the point at which the total gravitational torque on the body is zero
  3. ((c)) A couple on a body produce both translational and rotational motion in a body.
  4. ((d)) Mechanical advantage greater than one means that small effort can be used to lift a large load.

  2. (2)(c) and (d)
  3. (3)(b) and (d)

statements.label: (b)

solution.full_text: 1. Centre of mass may or may not coincide with centre of gravity.
solution.html: 1. Centre of mass may or may not coincide with centre of gravity.
steps: Centre of mass may or may not coincide with centre of gravity.
printed_lines: Centre of mass may or may not coincide with centre

steps: (a): The centre of mass coincides with the centre of gravity only when $\vec g$ is uniform over the body, so 'always' makes (a) false.

(b): The total gravitational torque $\sum \vec r_i \times m_i \vec g$ vanishes about the centre of gravity; for uniform $\vec g$ this is $\left(\sum m_i \vec r_i\right) \times \vec g = 0$ about the centre of mass, so (b) is taken as true.
(c): A couple is two equal and opposite forces, so $\vec F_{net} = 0$ and there is no translational motion, only rotation; (c) is false.
(d): $\text{M.A.} = \frac{\text{Load}}{\text{Effort}} > 1 \Rightarrow \text{Effort} < \text{Load}$, so a small effort lifts a large load; (d) is true.
The correct statements are (b) and (d), which is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:
1. (a): The centre of mass coincides with the centre of gravity only when →g is uniform over the body, so 'always' makes (a) false.
  2. (b): The total gravitational torque ∑ →ri × mi →g vanishes about the centre of gravity; for uniform →g this is (∑ mi →ri) × →g = 0 about the centre of mass, so (b) is taken as true.
  3. (c): A couple is two equal and opposite forces, so →Fnet = 0 and there is no translational motion, only rotation; (c) is false.
  4. (d): M.A. = LoadEffort > 1 ⇒ Effort < Load, so a small effort lifts a large load; (d) is true.
  5. The correct statements are (b) and (d), which is option 3.
ai_solution.why: (a) false (CM = CG only in a uniform field), (c) false (a couple produces only rotation), (d) true; (b) is the only remaining statement that can pair with (d), so (b) and (d).

solution.full_text:
1. $\varepsilon = -N\frac{d\phi}{dt}$
2. $\left|\frac{\varepsilon}{R}\right| = \frac{N}{R}\frac{d\phi}{dt}$
3. $dq = \frac{N}{R}d\phi$
4. $\Delta Q = \frac{N(\Delta\phi)}{R}$
5. $\Delta Q = \frac{\Delta\phi_{\mathrm{total}}}{R}$
6. $= \frac{(NBA)}{R}$
7. $= \frac{\mu_{0}ni\pi r^{2}}{R}$
8. Putting values
9. $= \frac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 100 \times 4 \times \pi \times (0.01)^{2}}{10\pi^{2}}$
10. $\Delta Q = 32\,\mu\mathrm{C}$
solution.html:
1. ε = -Ndφdt
  2. |εR| = NRdφdt
  3. dq = NRdφ
  4. Δ Q = N(Δφ)R
  5. Δ Q = ΔφtotalR
  6. = (NBA)R
  7. = μ0niπ r2R
  8. Putting values
  9. = 4π × 10-7 × 100 × 4 × π × (0.01)210π2
  10. Δ Q = 32 μC
steps: $\varepsilon = -N\frac{d\phi}{dt}$
$\left|\frac{\varepsilon}{R}\right| = \frac{N}{R}\frac{d\phi}{dt}$
$dq = \frac{N}{R}d\phi$
$\Delta Q = \frac{N(\Delta\phi)}{R}$
$\Delta Q = \frac{\Delta\phi_{\mathrm{total}}}{R}$
$= \frac{(NBA)}{R}$
$= \frac{\mu_{0}ni\pi r^{2}}{R}$
Putting values
$= \frac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 100 \times 4 \times \pi \times (0.01)^{2}}{10\pi^{2}}$
$\Delta Q = 32\,\mu\mathrm{C}$
Field inside the long solenoid: $B = \mu_0 n I$, uniform over the coil since the coil radius $0.01\,\mathrm{m}$ is less than the solenoid radius $0.05\,\mathrm{m}$.
Flux linkage through the coil: $N\Phi = N \mu_0 n I \pi r^2$.
Change in flux linkage as $I$ goes from $4\,\mathrm{A}$ to $0$: $\Delta(N\Phi) = 100 \times 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 2 \times 10^{4} \times 4 \times \pi (0.01)^2$.
Evaluate: $\Delta(N\Phi) = 3.2\pi^2 \times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{Wb}$.
Charge through the coil: $Q = \frac{\Delta(N\Phi)}{R} = \frac{3.2\pi^2 \times 10^{-4}}{10\pi^2}$.
$Q = 3.2 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{C} = 32\,\mu\mathrm{C}$, which is option $1$.

question.stem: The ratio of wavelengths of the last line of Balmer series and the last line of Lyman series is

solution.full_text:
1. For last Balmer series
2. $\frac{1}{\lambda_b} = R\left[\frac{1}{2^2} - \frac{1}{\infty^2}\right]$
3. $\lambda_b = \frac{4}{R}$
4. For last Lyman series
5. $\frac{1}{\lambda_l} = R\left[\frac{1}{1^2} - \frac{1}{\infty^2}\right]$
6. $\lambda_l = \frac{1}{R}$
7. $\frac{\lambda_b}{\lambda_l} = \frac{\frac{4}{R}}{\frac{1}{R}}$
8. $\frac{\lambda_b}{\lambda_l} = 4$
solution.html:
1. For last Balmer series
  2. 1λb = R[122 - 1∞2]
  3. λb = 4R
  4. For last Lyman series
  5. 1λl = R[112 - 1∞2]
  6. λl = 1R
  7. λbλl = 4R1R
  8. λbλl = 4
steps: For last Balmer series
$\frac{1}{\lambda_b} = R\left[\frac{1}{2^2} - \frac{1}{\infty^2}\right]$
$\lambda_b = \frac{4}{R}$
For last Lyman series
$\frac{1}{\lambda_l} = R\left[\frac{1}{1^2} - \frac{1}{\infty^2}\right]$
$\lambda_l = \frac{1}{R}$
$\frac{\lambda_b}{\lambda_l} = \frac{\frac{4}{R}}{\frac{1}{R}}$
$\frac{\lambda_b}{\lambda_l} = 4$
The last line of a series is its series limit, the transition from $n_i = \infty$.
Balmer limit: $\frac{1}{\lambda_B} = R\left(\frac{1}{2^2} - \frac{1}{\infty^2}\right) = \frac{R}{4}$, so $\lambda_B = \frac{4}{R}$.
Lyman limit: $\frac{1}{\lambda_L} = R\left(\frac{1}{1^2} - \frac{1}{\infty^2}\right) = R$, so $\lambda_L = \frac{1}{R}$.
$\frac{\lambda_B}{\lambda_L} = \frac{4/R}{1/R} = 4$, which is option $1$.

  2. Balmer limit: 1λB = R(122 - 1∞2) = R4, so λB = 4R.
  3. Lyman limit: 1λL = R(112 - 1∞2) = R, so λL = 1R.
  4. λBλL = 4/R1/R = 4, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: Last lines are series limits (n = infinity): lambda_Balmer = 4/R, lambda_Lyman = 1/R, so the ratio is 4.

question.stem: Suppose the charge of a proton and an electron differ slightly. One of them is $-e$, the other is $(e + \Delta e)$. If the net of electrostatic force and gravitational force between two hydrogen atoms placed at a distance $d$ (much greater than atomic size) apart is zero, then $\Delta e$ is of the order of [Given mass of hydrogen $m_h = 1.67 \times 10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}$]

solution.full_text:
1. $F_e = F_g$
2. $\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{\Delta e^2}{d^2} = \frac{Gm^2}{d^2}$
3. $9 \times 10^{9}\,(\Delta e^2) = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 1.67 \times 10^{-27} \times 1.67 \times 10^{-27}$
4. $\Delta e^2 = \frac{6.67 \times 1.67 \times 1.67}{9} \times 10^{-74}$
5. $\Delta e \approx 10^{-37}$
solution.html:
1. Fe = Fg
  2. 14πε0Δ e2d2 = Gm2d2
  3. 9 × 109 (Δ e2) = 6.67 × 10-11 × 1.67 × 10-27 × 1.67 × 10-27
  4. Δ e2 = 6.67 × 1.67 × 1.679 × 10-74
  5. Δ e ≈ 10-37
steps: $F_e = F_g$
$\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{\Delta e^2}{d^2} = \frac{Gm^2}{d^2}$
$\Delta e^2 = \frac{6.67 \times 1.67 \times 1.67}{9} \times 10^{-74}$
$\Delta e \approx 10^{-37}$
Each hydrogen atom has net charge $q = (e + \Delta e) - e = \Delta e$.
Electrostatic repulsion between the atoms: $F_e = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{(\Delta e)^2}{d^2}$.
Gravitational attraction between the atoms: $F_g = \frac{G m_h^2}{d^2}$.
Net force zero means $F_e = F_g$, so $\frac{(\Delta e)^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} = G m_h^2$.
$\Delta e = m_h\sqrt{4\pi\varepsilon_0 G} = m_h\sqrt{\frac{G}{k}}$ with $k = 9\times10^{9}\,\mathrm{N\,m^2\,C^{-2}}$.
$\Delta e \approx 1.67\times10^{-27} \times 8.6\times10^{-11} \approx 1.44\times10^{-37}\,\mathrm{C}$, of the order $10^{-37}\,\mathrm{C}$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Each hydrogen atom has net charge q = (e + Δ e) - e = Δ e.
  2. Electrostatic repulsion between the atoms: Fe = 14πε0(Δ e)2d2.
  3. Gravitational attraction between the atoms: Fg = G mh2d2.
  4. Net force zero means Fe = Fg, so (Δ e)24πε0 = G mh2.
  5. Δ e = mh4πε0 G = mhGk with k = 9×109 N m2 C-2.
  6. 6.67×10-119×109 = 7.41×10-21 ≈ 8.6×10-11.
  7. Δ e ≈ 1.67×10-27 × 8.6×10-11 ≈ 1.44×10-37 C, of the order 10-37 C, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: Each H atom carries net charge Δe; equating kΔe²/d² = Gm²/d² gives Δe = m√(G/k) ≈ 1.4 × 10^-37 C.

chapter.name: Electrostatics
chapter.why: The answer comes from setting the Coulomb force between the two atoms' net charges, k(Δe)^2/d^2, equal to the Newtonian gravitational attraction Gm_h^2/d^2 and solving for Δe, so it needs both Coulomb's law and the universal law of gravitation.

subtopics.name: Coulomb's Law
subtopics.why: The answer comes from setting the Coulomb force between the net charges Δe of the two atoms, kΔe²/d², equal to the gravitational force Gm_h²/d², which gives Δe ~ 10^-37 C.

step_list: Realise that each hydrogen atom (one proton, one electron) is no longer neutral but carries a net charge of magnitude delta-e
Equate the Coulomb repulsion k(delta-e)^2/d^2 between the two atoms to the gravitational attraction G m_h^2/d^2, noting d^2 cancels
Solve for delta-e = m_h * sqrt(G/k), recalling G = 6.67e-11 and k = 9e9 SI since neither is given
Evaluate the powers of ten (G/k ~ 7e-21, its square root ~ 9e-11, times 1.67e-27) to get the order of magnitude
difficulty.why: The work is a modelling step (net atomic charge equals delta-e) followed by a force balance between Coulomb and gravitational laws, an algebraic rearrangement with a square root, and an order-of-magnitude evaluation using constants the candidate must supply from memory.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: The key insight that each atom carries net charge delta-e is not stated; G and k are not given; and the 10^-47 C option is exactly m_h*G/k, the result of forgetting to take the square root, so a plausible wrong route lands on a listed option.

source.note: Text-layer draft dropped the Greek Delta: it reads '(e + e)' and 'then e is of the order of', but the image clearly prints '(e + \u0394e)' and '\u0394e'; transcribed from the image. No stacked fraction bars are visible in the crop despite the needs_image_read flag.

categories.concept: Setting the Coulomb repulsion of two charges $\Delta e$ equal to the gravitational attraction of two hydrogen masses gives $\Delta e=m_h\sqrt{G/k}$, with the separation cancelling out

trap.label: arithmetic_slip
trap.route: Leaving the square root off $\frac{G}{k}$ gives $m_h\frac{G}{k}=1.67\times10^{-27}\times7.4\times10^{-21}\approx10^{-47}$ C instead of $m_h\sqrt{G/k}\approx10^{-37}$ C.
trap.who: a student who sets up $\frac{k(\Delta e)^2}{d^2}=\frac{Gm_h^2}{d^2}$ correctly and then reads $\Delta e$ off without taking the root of both sides
trap.feels: every physical step has been done right and the awkward powers of ten in G and k have been handled, so an exponent in the forties looks like what numbers this small should give

steps.text: $\frac{k(\Delta e)^2}{d^2}=\frac{Gm_h^2}{d^2}$, so $(\Delta e)^2=\frac{G}{k}m_h^2$, with $\frac{G}{k}=\frac{6.67\times10^{-11}}{9\times10^{9}}=7.4\times10^{-21}$.
So $\Delta e=m_h\times7.4\times10^{-21}=1.2\times10^{-47}$ C.
steps.fix: Take the square root of both sides: $\Delta e=m_h\sqrt{7.4\times10^{-21}}=1.67\times10^{-27}\times8.6\times10^{-11}\approx1.4\times10^{-37}$ C.

other_options.who: a student who writes the gravitational force with one mass instead of the product of the two
other_options.feels: both atoms are hydrogen, so a single $m_h$ reads as 'the mass of hydrogen' already accounted for in the formula

steps.text: Equate the two forces, and the $d^2$ cancels from both sides.
Write $k(\Delta e)^2=Gm_h$, giving $\Delta e=\sqrt{\frac{6.67\times10^{-11}\times1.67\times10^{-27}}{9\times10^{9}}}=3.5\times10^{-24}$ C, whose nearest printed order is $10^{-23}$ C.
steps.fix: Newton's law needs both masses: $F=\frac{Gm_hm_h}{d^2}$, so $m_h$ enters squared and the square root leaves one factor of $m_h$ behind.

other_options.proof: The quantities the stem's numbers build are $\sqrt{G/k}=8.6\times10^{-11}$, $m_h\sqrt{G/k}=1.4\times10^{-37}$ (correct), $m_h\frac{G}{k}=1.2\times10^{-47}$ (root dropped), $\sqrt{Gm_h/k}=3.5\times10^{-24}$ (one mass dropped) and $\frac{Gm_h^2}{k}=1.2\times10^{-74}$. $10^{-20}$ C is none of these; it sits just above the electronic charge $1.6\times10^{-19}$ C in order of magnitude, a quantity the stem never asks for.

categories.reason: This question requires balancing Coulomb's law against gravitation for two hydrogen atoms, demonstrated by the stem asking what order $\Delta e$ is 'if the net of electrostatic force and gravitational force between two hydrogen atoms ... is zero'.

spec.title: Inputs A and B through a NOR gate, then a NOR gate with both inputs tied together, then a NOT gate to output Y

solution.full_text: 1. $Y = \overline{A + B}$
solution.html: 1. Y = A + B
steps: $Y = \overline{A + B}$
First gate is a NOR: $Y_1 = \overline{A + B}$.
Second NOR has both inputs tied to $Y_1$, so it acts as NOT: $Y_2 = \overline{Y_1 + Y_1} = \overline{Y_1} = A + B$.
Third gate is a NOT: $Y = \overline{Y_2} = \overline{A + B}$.
$Y = \overline{A + B}$ is the NOR function, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. First gate is a NOR: Y1 = A + B.
  2. Second NOR has both inputs tied to Y1, so it acts as NOT: Y2 = Y1 + Y1 = Y1 = A + B.
  3. Third gate is a NOT: Y = Y2 = A + B.
  4. Y = A + B is the NOR function, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: NOR(A,B) fed to a NOR with tied inputs (acts as NOT) gives A+B, then the final NOT gives (A+B)' = NOR.

categories.concept: A NOR gate with its two inputs tied together acts as a NOT gate, so the two inversions following the first NOR cancel and the network is a NOR

trap.label: reversed
trap.route: Missing the bubble on the middle gate turns it into a pass-through, which leaves the final NOT cancelling the first gate's bubble and the output reading as OR — the exact complement of the right gate.
trap.who: a student who traces the figure stage by stage but reads the second gate's tied inputs as a repeater
trap.feels: the second gate has one signal going in and one coming out, which looks like a buffer, and a NOT after a NOR cancels neatly to OR

steps.text: The first gate is an OR body with a bubble, so its output is $\overline{A+B}$.
The middle gate just passes that on, and the final NOT then undoes the first bubble, giving $A+B$ — an OR gate.
steps.fix: The middle gate carries a bubble too: with both inputs tied it gives $\overline{X+X}=\overline{X}$, so there are two inversions after the first gate and they cancel each other, leaving NOR.

other_options.who: a student who settles the network by counting inversion bubbles along the chain
other_options.feels: three bubbles in a row is an odd number of inversions, which reads as one net inversion

steps.text: Each bubble in the figure inverts the signal, and there are three of them.
Three inversions come to one inversion, so the network is a NOT gate.
steps.fix: A NOT gate takes one input; this network takes A and B separately and the first stage combines them with an OR before anything is inverted.

other_options.who: a student who applies De Morgan to the first stage and then names the operator standing in front of them
other_options.feels: $\overline{A+B}=\overline{A}\cdot\overline{B}$ puts a product on the page, and a product reads as AND

steps.text: The first gate gives $\overline{A+B}$, which De Morgan rewrites as $\overline{A}\cdot\overline{B}$.
The dot means the network is equivalent to an AND gate.
steps.fix: An AND gate gives $A\cdot B$; $\overline{A}\cdot\overline{B}$ is just NOR written another way, and the two later inversions cancel rather than change it.

question.full_text:
A Carnot engine having an efficiency of $\frac{1}{10}$ as heat engine, is used as a refrigerator. If the work done on the system is $10\,\mathrm{J}$, the amount of energy absorbed from the reservoir at lower temperature is
(1) $99\,\mathrm{J}$
(2) $100\,\mathrm{J}$
(3) $1\,\mathrm{J}$
(4) $90\,\mathrm{J}$
question.html:
A Carnot engine having an efficiency of 110 as heat engine, is used as a refrigerator. If the work done on the system is 10 J, the amount of energy absorbed from the reservoir at lower temperature is
  1. (1)99 J
  2. (2)100 J
  3. (3)1 J
  4. (4)90 J
question.stem: A Carnot engine having an efficiency of $\frac{1}{10}$ as heat engine, is used as a refrigerator. If the work done on the system is $10\,\mathrm{J}$, the amount of energy absorbed from the reservoir at lower temperature is

solution.html:
1. β = 1-ηη
  2. = 1-110110 = 910110
  3. β = 9
  4. β = Q2W
  5. Q2 = 9 × 10 = 90 J
steps: $\beta = \frac{1-\eta}{\eta}$
$\beta = 9$
$\beta = \frac{Q_2}{W}$
$Q_2 = 9 \times 10 = 90\,\mathrm{J}$
Engine efficiency: $\eta = 1 - \frac{T_2}{T_1} = \frac{1}{10}$, so $\frac{T_2}{T_1} = \frac{9}{10}$.
Coefficient of performance of the same Carnot cycle run as a refrigerator: $\beta = \frac{T_2}{T_1 - T_2} = \frac{1-\eta}{\eta}$.
Heat absorbed from the cold reservoir: $Q_2 = \beta W = 9 \times 10\,\mathrm{J} = 90\,\mathrm{J}$, which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Engine efficiency: η = 1 - T2T1 = 110, so T2T1 = 910.
  2. Coefficient of performance of the same Carnot cycle run as a refrigerator: β = T2T1 - T2 = 1-ηη.
  3. β = 9/101/10 = 9.
  4. Heat absorbed from the cold reservoir: Q2 = β W = 9 × 10 J = 90 J, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: For a reversed Carnot engine, COP beta = (1 - eta)/eta = 9, so heat absorbed from the cold reservoir Q2 = beta x W = 9 x 10 = 90 J.

step_list: Recognise that the Carnot engine run in reverse as a refrigerator has the same W, Q_hot and Q_cold magnitudes (or equivalently that its COP is (1 - eta)/eta)
Use eta = W/Q_hot with the given efficiency and work to find the heat exchanged with the hot reservoir
Apply energy conservation Q_cold = Q_hot - W to get the heat absorbed from the cold reservoir
difficulty.why: The work is linking engine efficiency to the reversed cycle, getting Q_hot from eta = W/Q_hot, and then subtracting W by energy balance to reach Q_cold.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: One distractor equals Q_hot, the heat rejected to the hot reservoir, so a candidate who confuses which reservoir the question asks about, or stops after the efficiency step, lands on a listed option.

source.note: Read from image. Efficiency is printed as a stacked fraction 1/10; the text-layer draft had split it ('1 36. 10') and carried a stray trailing '1' after 'is', which is not in the image. Stem ends at 'is' with no punctuation, as printed.

categories.concept: Run backwards, a Carnot engine of efficiency $\eta$ has coefficient of performance $\frac{1-\eta}{\eta}$, so the heat drawn from the cold reservoir is $W\left(\frac{1}{\eta}-1\right)$

trap.label: answers_other_question
trap.route: 100 J is the heat delivered to the HOT reservoir, $\frac{W}{\eta}$, which the same calculation produces; the stem asks for the heat taken in at the lower temperature, which is 100 J less the 10 J of work.
trap.who: a student who computes $\frac{W}{\eta}=\frac{10}{0.1}$ and reads the first number the efficiency yields as the answer
trap.feels: $\frac{W}{\eta}$ is the one step an efficiency of $\frac{1}{10}$ invites, and 100 J is the round number it gives

steps.text: An efficiency of $\frac{1}{10}$ ties the work to the heat at the hot reservoir: $Q_H=\frac{W}{\eta}=100$ J.
So the energy absorbed from the lower-temperature reservoir is 100 J.
steps.fix: 100 J is what the refrigerator dumps into the hot reservoir; take off the 10 J of work done on it, leaving $Q_C=90$ J.

other_options.who: a student who multiplies by the efficiency where the relation divides
other_options.feels: an efficiency of one tenth suggests the answer should be a tenth of the 10 J of work

steps.text: The efficiency $\frac{1}{10}$ is the quantity that links work and heat.
So the heat involved is $\eta W=0.1\times10=1$ J.
steps.fix: Heat is the larger quantity in a refrigerator: $Q_H=\frac{W}{\eta}$ and $Q_C=W\left(\frac{1}{\eta}-1\right)=90$ J.

other_options.proof: The quantities the stem's two numbers build are $\frac{W}{\eta}=100$ J, $W\left(\frac{1}{\eta}-1\right)=90$ J, $\eta W=1$ J and the coefficient of performance $\frac{1}{\eta}-1=9$. 99 J is none of them — it is the 100 J option less the 1 J option — and no single step of the Carnot relations produces it.

question.full_text:
In an electromagnetic wave in free space the root mean square value of the electric field is $E_{rms} = 6\,\mathrm{V/m}$. The peak value of the magnetic field is
(1) $0.70 \times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{T}$
(2) $4.23 \times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{T}$
(3) $1.41 \times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{T}$
(4) $2.83 \times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{T}$
question.html:
In an electromagnetic wave in free space the root mean square value of the electric field is Erms = 6 V/m. The peak value of the magnetic field is
  1. (1)0.70 × 10-8 T
  2. (2)4.23 × 10-8 T
  3. (3)1.41 × 10-8 T
  4. (4)2.83 × 10-8 T
question.stem: In an electromagnetic wave in free space the root mean square value of the electric field is $E_{rms} = 6\,\mathrm{V/m}$. The peak value of the magnetic field is

solution.full_text:
1. $\frac{E_{rms}}{B_{rms}} = c$
2. $B_{rms} = \frac{E_{rms}}{c}$
3. $= \frac{6}{3 \times 10^{8}}$
4. $B_{rms} = 2 \times 10^{-8}$
5. $B_{rms} = \frac{B_0}{\sqrt{2}}$
6. $B_0 = \sqrt{2} \times B_{rms}$
7. $= \sqrt{2} \times 2 \times 10^{-8}$
8. $= 2.83 \times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{T}$
solution.html:
1. ErmsBrms = c
  2. Brms = Ermsc
  3. = 63 × 108
  4. Brms = 2 × 10-8
  5. Brms = B02
  6. B0 = 2 × Brms
  7. = 2 × 2 × 10-8
  8. = 2.83 × 10-8 T
steps: $\frac{E_{rms}}{B_{rms}} = c$
$B_{rms} = \frac{E_{rms}}{c}$
$B_{rms} = \frac{B_0}{\sqrt{2}}$
$B_0 = \sqrt{2} \times B_{rms}$
$= \sqrt{2} \times 2 \times 10^{-8}$
The peak electric field is $E_0 = \sqrt{2}\,E_{rms} = \sqrt{2} \times 6 \approx 8.485\,\mathrm{V/m}$.
In free space $B_0 = \frac{E_0}{c}$.
$B_0 = \frac{8.485}{3 \times 10^{8}} \approx 2.83 \times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{T}$, which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. The peak electric field is E0 = 2 Erms = 2 × 6 ≈ 8.485 V/m.
  2. In free space B0 = E0c.
  3. B0 = 8.4853 × 108 ≈ 2.83 × 10-8 T, which is option 4.

categories.concept: In an electromagnetic wave $B=\frac{E}{c}$ at every instant, and the peak value of a sinusoid is $\sqrt{2}$ times its rms value

trap.label: arithmetic_slip
trap.route: Dividing by $\sqrt{2}$ where it should be multiplied gives $\frac{6}{\sqrt{2}\times3\times10^{8}}=1.41\times10^{-8}$ T, with the $B=\frac{E}{c}$ step itself done correctly.
trap.who: a student who knows peak and rms differ by $\sqrt{2}$ and applies the factor in the direction that takes the number down
trap.feels: $\sqrt{2}$ is plainly the factor this question is about, and an answer reading $\sqrt{2}\times10^{-8}$ looks like the one that used it

steps.text: $B=\frac{E}{c}$, so the rms magnetic field is $\frac{6}{3\times10^{8}}=2\times10^{-8}$ T.
Convert to the peak by dividing by $\sqrt{2}$: $\frac{2\times10^{-8}}{1.41}=1.41\times10^{-8}$ T.
steps.fix: A peak is bigger than an rms value: multiply by $\sqrt{2}$, giving $2.83\times10^{-8}$ T.

other_options.who: a student who stores the peak as twice the rms rather than $\sqrt{2}$ times it
other_options.feels: doubling gives $4\times10^{-8}$ T and this is the only option anywhere near that value

steps.text: $B_{rms}=\frac{E_{rms}}{c}=\frac{6}{3\times10^{8}}=2\times10^{-8}$ T.
Peak is twice rms, so $4\times10^{-8}$ T, and the option printing $4.23\times10^{-8}$ T is the one in that neighbourhood.
steps.fix: The peak-to-rms factor for a sinusoid is $\sqrt{2}$, not 2: $2\times10^{-8}\times1.414=2.83\times10^{-8}$ T.

other_options.proof: The four options are $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$, $\sqrt{2}$, $2\sqrt{2}$ and $3\sqrt{2}$ times $10^{-8}$ T, a grid in steps of $\sqrt{2}$. Every single named operation on 6 V/m and $3\times10^{8}$ m/s lands elsewhere: $\frac{E}{c}=2\times10^{-8}$, $\frac{\sqrt{2}E}{c}=2.83\times10^{-8}$, $\frac{E}{\sqrt{2}c}=1.41\times10^{-8}$, $\frac{E}{2c}=1\times10^{-8}$, $\frac{2E}{c}=4\times10^{-8}$. Reaching $0.70\times10^{-8}$ requires $\frac{E}{2\sqrt{2}c}$, that is the $\sqrt{2}$ divided twice over, which is no one step.

question.full_text:
Two Polaroids $P_1$ and $P_2$ are placed with their axis perpendicular to each other. Unpolarised light $I_0$ is incident on $P_1$. A third polaroid $P_3$ is kept in between $P_1$ and $P_2$ such that its axis makes an angle $45^\circ$ with that of $P_1$. The intensity of transmitted light through $P_2$ is
(1) $\dfrac{I_0}{8}$
(2) $\dfrac{I_0}{16}$
(3) $\dfrac{I_0}{2}$
(4) $\dfrac{I_0}{4}$
question.html:
Two Polaroids P1 and P2 are placed with their axis perpendicular to each other. Unpolarised light I0 is incident on P1. A third polaroid P3 is kept in between P1 and P2 such that its axis makes an angle 45° with that of P1. The intensity of transmitted light through P2 is
  1. (1)I08
  2. (2)I016
  3. (3)I02
  4. (4)I04
question.stem: Two Polaroids $P_1$ and $P_2$ are placed with their axis perpendicular to each other. Unpolarised light $I_0$ is incident on $P_1$. A third polaroid $P_3$ is kept in between $P_1$ and $P_2$ such that its axis makes an angle $45^\circ$ with that of $P_1$. The intensity of transmitted light through $P_2$ is

solution.full_text:
[Figure: Unpolarised light I0 passing through polaroids P1, P3 and P2, with the axes of P3 and P2 at 45 deg and 90 deg to the axis of P1]
1. $I_2 = \frac{I_0}{2}\cos^2 45^\circ$
2. $= \frac{I_0}{2} \times \frac{1}{2}$
3. $= \frac{I_0}{4}$
4. $I_3 = \frac{I_0}{4}\cos^2 45^\circ$
5. $I_3 = \frac{I_0}{8}$
solution.html:
1. I2 = I02cos2 45°
  2. = I02 × 12
  3. = I04
  4. I3 = I04cos2 45°
  5. I3 = I08
steps: $= \frac{I_0}{2} \times \frac{1}{2}$

figures.text: Unpolarised light I0 passing through polaroids P1, P3 and P2, with the axes of P3 and P2 at 45 deg and 90 deg to the axis of P1

checks.print_match: all 9 label(s) printed; 94% of the spec's lines on the printed ones, 93% of the printed lines covered

spec.title: Unpolarised light I0 passing through polaroids P1, P3 and P2, with the axes of P3 and P2 at 45 deg and 90 deg to the axis of P1

steps: Unpolarised light through $P_1$: $I_1 = \frac{I_0}{2}$.
$P_3$ makes $45^\circ$ with $P_1$, so by Malus's law $I_3 = I_1 \cos^2 45^\circ = \frac{I_0}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} = \frac{I_0}{4}$.
$P_2$ is perpendicular to $P_1$, so it makes $90^\circ - 45^\circ = 45^\circ$ with $P_3$.
$I_2 = I_3 \cos^2 45^\circ = \frac{I_0}{4} \times \frac{1}{2} = \frac{I_0}{8}$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Unpolarised light through P1: I1 = I02.
  2. P3 makes 45° with P1, so by Malus's law I3 = I1 cos2 45° = I02 × 12 = I04.
  3. P2 is perpendicular to P1, so it makes 90° - 45° = 45° with P3.
  4. I2 = I3 cos2 45° = I04 × 12 = I08, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: P1 halves unpolarised light; Malus's law at 45 deg for P3 and again at 45 deg for P2 gives I0/2 x 1/2 x 1/2 = I0/8.

question.full_text:
If $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ be the apparent angles of dip observed in two vertical planes at right angles to each other, then the true angle of dip $\theta$ is given by
(1) $\cot^2\theta = \cot^2\theta_1 - \cot^2\theta_2$
(2) $\tan^2\theta = \tan^2\theta_1 - \tan^2\theta_2$
(3) $\cot^2\theta = \cot^2\theta_1 + \cot^2\theta_2$
(4) $\tan^2\theta = \tan^2\theta_1 + \tan^2\theta_2$
question.html:
If θ1 and θ2 be the apparent angles of dip observed in two vertical planes at right angles to each other, then the true angle of dip θ is given by
  1. (1)cot2θ = cot2θ1 - cot2θ2
  2. (2)tan2θ = tan2θ1 - tan2θ2
  3. (3)cot2θ = cot2θ1 + cot2θ2
  4. (4)tan2θ = tan2θ1 + tan2θ2
question.stem: If $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ be the apparent angles of dip observed in two vertical planes at right angles to each other, then the true angle of dip $\theta$ is given by

solution.full_text: 1. $\cot^2\theta = \cot^2\theta_1 + \cot^2\theta_2$
solution.html: 1. cot2θ = cot2θ1 + cot2θ2
steps: $\cot^2\theta = \cot^2\theta_1 + \cot^2\theta_2$
True dip satisfies $\tan\theta = \frac{B_V}{B_H}$, so $\cot\theta = \frac{B_H}{B_V}$.

In a vertical plane at angle $\alpha$ to the magnetic meridian, the horizontal component is $B_H\cos\alpha$ while $B_V$ is unchanged, so $\tan\theta_1 = \frac{B_V}{B_H\cos\alpha}$, i.e. $\cot\theta_1 = \cot\theta\cos\alpha$.
In the perpendicular vertical plane the horizontal component is $B_H\sin\alpha$, so $\tan\theta_2 = \frac{B_V}{B_H\sin\alpha}$, i.e. $\cot\theta_2 = \cot\theta\sin\alpha$.
Squaring and adding: $\cot^2\theta_1 + \cot^2\theta_2 = \cot^2\theta(\cos^2\alpha + \sin^2\alpha) = \cot^2\theta$.
Hence $\cot^2\theta = \cot^2\theta_1 + \cot^2\theta_2$, which is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:
1. True dip satisfies tanθ = BVBH, so cotθ = BHBV.
  2. In a vertical plane at angle α to the magnetic meridian, the horizontal component is BHcosα while BV is unchanged, so tanθ1 = BVBHcosα, i.e. cotθ1 = cotθcosα.
  3. In the perpendicular vertical plane the horizontal component is BHsinα, so tanθ2 = BVBHsinα, i.e. cotθ2 = cotθsinα.
  4. Squaring and adding: cot2θ1 + cot2θ2 = cot2θ(cos2α + sin2α) = cot2θ.
  5. Hence cot2θ = cot2θ1 + cot2θ2, which is option 3.
ai_solution.why: In a plane at angle alpha to the meridian, cot(theta1) = cot(theta) cos(alpha) and in the perpendicular plane cot(theta2) = cot(theta) sin(alpha); squaring and adding gives cot^2(theta) = cot^2(theta1) + cot^2(theta2).

subtopics.name: Earth's Magnetism
subtopics.why: The answer is the relation cot^2(theta) = cot^2(theta1) + cot^2(theta2) between true and apparent angles of dip, which is an element of Earth's magnetism.

step_list: For a vertical plane at angle alpha to the magnetic meridian, keep the vertical component V unchanged and resolve the horizontal component to H cos(alpha), writing the apparent dip theta1 as the ratio of V to that effective horizontal component
Repeat for the perpendicular plane, where the effective horizontal component is H sin(alpha), giving the corresponding expression for theta2

Combine the two expressions to eliminate the unknown alpha via sin^2(alpha) + cos^2(alpha) = 1, identify the surviving ratio with the true dip (tan theta = V/H), and match against the tan/cot, sum/difference option forms
difficulty.why: The work is resolving the horizontal field component into two perpendicular vertical planes, writing the apparent-dip ratio for each, and eliminating the unknown orientation angle with a trigonometric identity.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: Apparent dip is not treated in NCERT and the Earth's magnetism section is absent from the current rationalised NCERT, so the resolution must be built without textbook support; the options form a tan/cot x sum/difference grid, so inverting the dip ratio (horizontal over vertical) leads straight to a matching wrong form.

categories.concept: Apparent dip always exceeds the true dip, and for two vertical planes at right angles the cotangent squares add: $\cot^2\theta=\cot^2\theta_1+\cot^2\theta_2$

trap.label: formula_misused
trap.route: Dip is defined by $\tan\theta=B_V/B_H$, so a student holding 'dip is a tangent' writes the additive rule in tangents and reads off $\tan^2\theta=\tan^2\theta_1+\tan^2\theta_2$; it is the horizontal component that splits between the two planes, so the cotangents are what add.
trap.who: a student who knows $\tan\theta=B_V/B_H$ and remembers the two-plane result only as 'the squares add'
trap.feels: the option has the same additive shape as the correct relation, and $\tan$ is the function the definition of dip is stated in

steps.text: Dip obeys $\tan\theta=B_V/B_H$, and in a plane at angle $\alpha$ to the meridian the horizontal component is only $B_H\cos\alpha$.
Since the squares add, write the rule in the function dip is defined in: $\tan^2\theta=\tan^2\theta_1+\tan^2\theta_2$.
steps.fix: $\tan\theta_1=\tan\theta/\cos\alpha$ and $\tan\theta_2=\tan\theta/\sin\alpha$, so it is $\cot^2\theta_1+\cot^2\theta_2$ that sums to $\cot^2\theta$.

other_options.who: a student who has the cotangent form of the result but recalls the two planes as combining by subtraction
other_options.feels: the cotangents are the right function, and both apparent dips come out larger than the true dip, which reads as though something has to be taken away

steps.text: Write the relation in cotangents, since $\cot\theta=B_H/B_V$ and it is $B_H$ that the two planes share out.
Because each apparent dip is larger than the true dip, subtract: $\cot^2\theta=\cot^2\theta_1-\cot^2\theta_2$.
steps.fix: The step that closes the derivation is $\cos^2\alpha+\sin^2\alpha=1$, so the two cotangent squares are added.

other_options.proof: Worked the derivation through: $\tan\theta_1=\tan\theta/\cos\alpha$, $\tan\theta_2=\tan\theta/\sin\alpha$ and $\cos^2\alpha+\sin^2\alpha=1$ give a sum of cotangent squares. No step in it produces a difference, and the tangent reflex coming from $\tan\theta=B_V/B_H$ produces the sum printed in option 4, so no single remembered step yields tangents and a minus sign together.

categories.reason: This question requires the composition rule for two perpendicular apparent dips to be reproduced in the right trigonometric function and with the right sign, demonstrated by the four options printing the same relation as either $\cot^2$ or $\tan^2$ with either a plus or a minus.

question.full_text:
A 250-Turn rectangular coil of length $2.1\,\mathrm{cm}$ and width $1.25\,\mathrm{cm}$ carries a current of $85\,\mu\mathrm{A}$ and subjected to a magnetic field of strength $0.85\,\mathrm{T}$. Work done for rotating the coil by $180^\circ$ against the torque is
(1) $2.3\,\mu\mathrm{J}$
(2) $1.15\,\mu\mathrm{J}$
(3) $9.1\,\mu\mathrm{J}$
(4) $4.55\,\mu\mathrm{J}$
question.html:
A 250-Turn rectangular coil of length 2.1 cm and width 1.25 cm carries a current of 85 μA and subjected to a magnetic field of strength 0.85 T. Work done for rotating the coil by 180° against the torque is
  1. (1)2.3 μJ
  2. (2)1.15 μJ
  3. (3)9.1 μJ
  4. (4)4.55 μJ
question.stem: A 250-Turn rectangular coil of length $2.1\,\mathrm{cm}$ and width $1.25\,\mathrm{cm}$ carries a current of $85\,\mu\mathrm{A}$ and subjected to a magnetic field of strength $0.85\,\mathrm{T}$. Work done for rotating the coil by $180^\circ$ against the torque is

solution.full_text:
1. $W = MB(\cos\theta_1 - \cos\theta_2)$
2. When it is rotated by angle $180^\circ$ then
3. $W = 2MB$
4. $W = 2(NIA)B$
5. $= 2 \times 250 \times 85 \times 10^{-6}[1.25 \times 2.1 \times 10^{-4}] \times 85 \times 10^{-2}$
6. $= 9.1\,\mu\mathrm{J}$
solution.html:
1. W = MB(cosθ1 - cosθ2)
  2. When it is rotated by angle 180° then
  3. W = 2MB
  4. W = 2(NIA)B
  5. = 2 × 250 × 85 × 10-6[1.25 × 2.1 × 10-4] × 85 × 10-2
  6. = 9.1 μJ
steps: $W = MB(\cos\theta_1 - \cos\theta_2)$
When it is rotated by angle $180^\circ$ then
$W = 2MB$
$W = 2(NIA)B$
$= 2 \times 250 \times 85 \times 10^{-6}[1.25 \times 2.1 \times 10^{-4}] \times 85 \times 10^{-2}$
$= 9.1\,\mu\mathrm{J}$
printed_lines: When it is rotated by angle 180º then

steps: Area of the coil: $A = 2.1\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m} \times 1.25\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m} = 2.625\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m^2}$.
Magnetic moment: $m = NIA = 250 \times 85\times10^{-6} \times 2.625\times10^{-4} = 5.578\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{A\,m^2}$.
Work against the torque from $\theta = 0^\circ$ to $\theta = 180^\circ$: $W = U(180^\circ) - U(0^\circ) = -mB\cos 180^\circ + mB\cos 0^\circ = 2mB$.
$W = 2 \times 5.578\times10^{-6} \times 0.85 = 9.48\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{J} \approx 9.5\,\mu\mathrm{J}$.
The nearest option is $9.1\,\mu\mathrm{J}$, which is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Area of the coil: A = 2.1×10-2 m × 1.25×10-2 m = 2.625×10-4 m2.
  2. Magnetic moment: m = NIA = 250 × 85×10-6 × 2.625×10-4 = 5.578×10-6 A m2.
  3. Work against the torque from θ = 0° to θ = 180°: W = U(180°) - U(0°) = -mBcos 180° + mBcos 0° = 2mB.
  4. W = 2 × 5.578×10-6 × 0.85 = 9.48×10-6 J ≈ 9.5 μJ.
  5. The nearest option is 9.1 μJ, which is option 3.
ai_solution.why: Rotating the coil by 180 degrees from the stable position against the torque needs W = 2NIAB, which works out to about 9.5 uJ; the closest option is 9.1 uJ.

subtopics.name: Work Done or Potential Energy of a Current-Carrying Loop in a Uniform Magnetic Field
subtopics.why: The answer depends on the work done in rotating a current-carrying coil by 180 degrees in a uniform field, W = 2NIAB, which is taught under work done/potential energy of a current loop in a uniform magnetic field.

step_list: Compute the coil area A = length x width, converting cm x cm to m^2
Compute the magnetic moment m = N I A with I in microamperes converted to amperes
Apply W = change in potential energy = mB(cos 0 - cos 180) = 2mB, assuming the coil starts in stable equilibrium, and evaluate in microjoules
difficulty.why: The work is finding the coil's magnetic moment from N, I and area and then taking the change in its potential energy U = -mB cos(theta) over a 180 degree rotation, with unit conversions throughout.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: One option is exactly half of another, which is the result of using W = mB and forgetting the factor (1 - cos 180) = 2; the stem also leaves the starting orientation (aligned with the field) unstated.

source.note: Image shows micro prefix (\u03bc) on the current (85 \u03bcA) and on all four options (\u03bcJ); the text_layer_draft dropped the \u03bc (reads '85 A' and 'J'). Transcribed from the image.

categories.concept: Work done against the magnetic torque is the change in orientation energy $U=-MB\cos\theta$, so a $180^\circ$ turn costs $2MB$ with $M=NIA$

trap.label: arithmetic_slip
trap.route: Evaluating $MB=250\times85\,\mu\mathrm{A}\times2.625\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m^2}\times0.85\,\mathrm{T}$ and stopping there delivers half the work, because the coil starts at $-MB$ and ends at $+MB$, a gap of $2MB$; the printed $4.55\,\mu\mathrm{J}$ is exactly the key halved.
trap.who: a student who knows $U=-MB\cos\theta$ and evaluates it at the final orientation only
trap.feels: $MB$ is the full dipole-field product and uses every number in the stem once, and the minus sign looks as though it has already taken care of the half turn

steps.text: $M=NIA=250\times85\times10^{-6}\times2.625\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{A\,m^2}$, so $MB$ comes out at the $4.5\,\mu\mathrm{J}$ scale.
Take that $MB$ as the work for turning the coil through $180^\circ$.
steps.fix: $W=U_f-U_i=MB-(-MB)=2MB$, so the $MB$ just found has to be doubled.

other_options.proof: $2.3\,\mu\mathrm{J}$ is the key quartered. I checked the slips this calculation actually offers: dropping the doubling gives $4.55$, dropping the 250 turns divides by 250, leaving the area in $\mathrm{cm^2}$ multiplies by $10^4$, and reading $85\,\mu\mathrm{A}$ as $85\,\mathrm{A}$ multiplies by $10^6$. None of them scales the answer by 4, and the stem offers only one factor of 2 to drop.

$1.15\,\mu\mathrm{J}$ is the key divided by eight, the last term of the halving ladder $9.1, 4.55, 2.3, 1.15$. Running $W=2NIAB$ with each quantity in turn mis-scaled produces factors of 2, 250 or powers of ten, never a factor of 8, so no single wrong operation on the printed numbers lands here.

categories.reason: This question requires the orientation-energy difference for a half turn to be computed as $W=2NIAB$ from the stem's own numbers, demonstrated by the stem asking for 'Work done for rotating the coil by $180^\circ$ against the torque'.
categories.note: Substituting the printed numbers into $2NIAB$ gives $9.48\,\mu\mathrm{J}$ while the key prints $9.1\,\mu\mathrm{J}$; $9.1$ is the nearest option and the tag follows the printed key. The four options are that key successively halved ($9.1$, $4.55$, $2.3$, $1.15$), which is why every route here turns on the factor of 2.

question.full_text:
The resistance of a wire is '$R$' ohm. If it is melted and stretched to '$n$' times its original length, its new resistance will be
(1) $n^2R$
(2) $\dfrac{R}{n^2}$
(3) $nR$
(4) $\dfrac{R}{n}$
question.html:
The resistance of a wire is 'R' ohm. If it is melted and stretched to 'n' times its original length, its new resistance will be
  1. (1)n2R
  2. (2)Rn2
  3. (3)nR
  4. (4)Rn
question.stem: The resistance of a wire is '$R$' ohm. If it is melted and stretched to '$n$' times its original length, its new resistance will be

solution.html:
1. R2R1 = l22l12
  2. = n2 l12l12
  3. R2R1 = n2
  4. R2 = n2 R1

steps: Melting and stretching keeps the volume constant: $lA = (nl)A'$, so $A' = \frac{A}{n}$.
$R' = \frac{\rho (nl)}{A/n} = n^2 \frac{\rho l}{A}$.
Since $R = \frac{\rho l}{A}$, $R' = n^2 R$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Melting and stretching keeps the volume constant: lA = (nl)A', so A' = An.
  2. R' = ρ (nl)A/n = n2 ρ lA.
  3. Since R = ρ lA, R' = n2 R, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: Melting and recasting keeps the volume constant, so stretching length n times reduces area to A/n, giving R' = n^2 R.

chapter.name: Current Electricity
chapter.why: The answer n^2R depends on R = rho*l/A with volume held constant, so stretching n times multiplies length by n and divides area by n, which is the resistance/resistivity relation taught in Current Electricity.

subtopics.name: Resistance
subtopics.why: The answer n^2R follows from R = rho*L/A with volume held constant (A becomes A/n when L becomes nL), i.e. how a conductor's resistance depends on its length and cross-section.

step_list: Recognise that melting and re-drawing keeps the volume (and resistivity) constant, so stretching the length by a factor n shrinks the cross-sectional area by a factor n
Substitute both the new length and the new area into R = rho*l/A and combine the two factors to get the new resistance in terms of R and n
difficulty.why: The work is one recall of R = rho*l/A plus one application of volume conservation to change the area, then combining the length and area factors.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: Option (3) nR is exactly what a candidate gets by scaling only the length and forgetting that the area also changes.

source.note: Read from image; text-layer draft had stacked fractions in options 2 and 4 split into separate rows (R over n^2, R over n). Stem has no trailing punctuation as printed.

categories.concept: Melting and redrawing a wire keeps its volume, so stretching the length $n$ times thins the cross-section $n$ times and $R=\rho L/A$ rises by $n^2$

trap.label: condition_missed
trap.route: Reading only 'stretched to $n$ times its original length' and feeding it into $R=\rho L/A$ gives $nR$; the stem's word 'melted' fixes the volume, so the area drops to $A/n$ at the same time and the two factors multiply to $n^2$.

trap.feels: only the length is given a factor in the stem, so $R\propto L$ looks like the whole of the physics on offer

No area is mentioned, so leave $A$ as it was and write $nR$.
steps.fix: 'Melted and stretched' conserves the volume $AL$, so $A$ becomes $A/n$ and the resistance goes as $L^2$.

other_options.who: a student who gets the $n^2$ dependence out of the constant volume but forms the ratio with the old length over the new
other_options.feels: the right power of $n$ is already in the option, so only where it sits is left in question

steps.text: Constant volume gives $R\propto L^2$, so the two resistances differ by a factor $n^2$.
Write $R_{\text{new}}=R\left(L_{\text{old}}/L_{\text{new}}\right)^2=R/n^2$.
steps.fix: The redrawn wire is longer and thinner, so it must resist more: the factor multiplies, giving $n^2R$.

other_options.proof: Checked every single-step slip this stem offers: holding $A$ fixed gives $nR$, inverting the ratio gives $R/n^2$, and conserving the volume gives $n^2R$. $R/n$ needs $R\propto1/L$, which no reading of $R=\rho L/A$ supplies, so landing here takes the inversion and the loss of the area factor at once.
